title: Passive quantum memory
why: Gemini 4 Argon does most of the math for Stanford physicist Patrick Hayden, showing that a quantum memory can keep its data safe on its own, with no constant fixing, even when warm and jostled, a question open since Alexei Kitaev's early work on quantum computers.

title: Diffie–Hellman problem
why: Working with Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5, Yuwen Zhou drops a condition from Ueli Maurer's 30-year-old result, showing that breaking a basic way computers agree on secret keys is as hard as the math problem behind it, given a short hint.

title: Non-overlapping codes
why: Simon Blackburn proves the most code words possible when no word's ending can match the start of any word, beating Vladimir Levenshtein's 1970 limit, with GPT-6 Astra writing one of the paper's key proofs.

title: Frostbite
why: Architect Labs' AI agents design a new computer processor on their own, from its basic commands to the chip layout; in simulation it does 4.59 times as much work per watt as a comparable modern design.

title: Smoktunowicz's gap theorem
why: Working alone for 94 minutes, GPT-6.2 Astra writes the first computer-checked proof of a 2006 theorem by mathematician Agata Smoktunowicz about how fast certain kinds of algebra can grow, taking its own route rather than hers.

title: El-Zahar–Erdős conjecture
why: Chenghua Liu and Boning Meng, working with GPT-6, answer a 1985 question of Mohamed El-Zahar and Paul Erdős with a no: networks that need many colors so linked dots differ, yet never split into two unlinked parts that each need many.

title: Stafford's conjecture
why: AI agents write the first full proof of Toby Stafford's 1978 claim about an algebra used in quantum physics and have a computer check every step, for Christopher Albert, Johanna Moser and Maximilian Philipp.

title: McKay–Praeger conjecture
why: Ning Su and Binzhou Xia, working with GPT-6, prove that almost every network where all points look alike is built from a set of symmetries, as Brendan McKay and Cheryl Praeger predicted.

title: Sample compression
why: Google's Cogentic agents running Gemini 4 Carbon prove on their own that anything a machine can learn can be captured in a handful of examples, about the square of the task's difficulty, the first such limit for a question Sally Floyd and Manfred Warmuth posed in 1995.

title: Additive squares
why: GPT-6 writes almost all of a paper for Jeffrey Shallit that solves a problem open over 50 years: an endless string of just six numbers where no two side-by-side stretches share both length and total, checked by computer.

title: Bounded integer programming
why: Given two earlier papers by Lin Chen, Yuchen Mao and Guochuan Zhang, GPT-6 finds a faster way than theirs to pick the best whole numbers within limits, a basic planning problem, with almost no human help.

title: QMA and QCMA
why: With GPT-6 Astra writing nearly the entire proof, Yiming Wang shows a case where evidence held in a quantum computer can convince a checker of things that no amount of ordinary written evidence can.

title: Cubic Schrödinger equation
why: Xi Chen, working with ChatGPT 6, builds waves on a square with wrap-around edges whose energy keeps moving into ever smaller ripples without end, answering a question of Jean Bourgain.

title: nginx2root
why: With no human guidance, Xint's AI finds four flaws that let attackers take over servers running nginx, the software behind about a third of websites; a Xint researcher found a fifth, hidden since 2015.

title: GPU chip design
why: OpenAI's models redesign parts of AMD's top graphics chip for up to 14% better speed, power use and size, about a year of engineering in under five months; AMD puts some of the changes in a chip it has sent to be made.

title: Topological overlap
why: GPT-6 Astra, following Sergey Norin's directions, determines the topological overlap constant in every dimension. It equals the affine constant, confirming a conjecture of Boris Bukh, Jiří Matoušek and Gabriel Nivasch.

title: Shortest paths on 4-polytopes
why: Igor Pak, working with ChatGPT, proves that computing geodesic distance on the boundary of a convex 4-polytope is NP-hard. He also builds polytopes with exponentially many shortest paths between two points, disproving several conjectures.

title: Positroid conjecture
why: ChatGPT-6 Astra proves Ehrhart positivity for integral polypositroids, settling the positroid conjecture of Luis Ferroni, Katharina Jochemko and Benjamin Schröter. Ferroni steered its 117-page first proof; ChatGPT-6.2 Astra simplified it and Claude Opus 5.5 checked it.

title: Navier–Stokes blowup
why: Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, working with Claude, construct smooth, compactly supported initial data for which the unforced 3D Navier–Stokes equations blow up in finite time. The accompanying Lean library runs to about 600,000 lines.

title: Euler blowup
why: With Matei Coiculescu, Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster prove finite-time singularity formation for the 3D incompressible Euler equations from smooth periodic data: vorticity becomes infinite at the origin while velocity stays bounded. They used Claude and Codex throughout; the proof is formalized in Lean.

title: McEliece challenges
why: MiniMax's unreleased model recovers secret keys for 55 unsolved McEliece challenge instances. It also gives the first practical breaks of several withdrawn NIST post-quantum candidates.

title: Metal–organic frameworks
why: MOFGen, an agent system from Théo Jaffrelot Inizan, Kristin Persson and Omar Yaghi, proposes new metal–organic frameworks for CO₂ capture and water harvesting. Four are synthesized.

title: MONAI Label zero-day
why: AI agents run by China-linked actors find a zero-day in MONAI Label, a medical-imaging annotation tool, then use it to take over a university server with minimal human direction.

title: Masullo's GRH proof
why: Within hours of Ravi Vakil posting Alessandro Masullo's claimed proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis, several mathematicians use AI to identify problems in it.

title: Valiant's conjecture
why: An internal Claude model proves that VP and VNP are distinct over every field, with a Lean formalization. OpenAI posts an independent proof hours later.

title: Auction pricing limits
why: Gemini 4 resolves the subadditive prophet inequality, asked by Michal Feldman, Nick Gravin and Brendan Lucier in 2015. Posted prices achieve a nearly tight triple-logarithmic approximation; no constant factor is possible.

title: Open MIPLIB instances
why: A single GPT-6.2 Astra agent per problem proves optimality for six of ten open MIPLIB instances, in 10 to 136 minutes each, for Dmitry Rybin of AutoKernel. It also improves the best known solutions to three.

title: Smale's ninth problem
why: An internal OpenAI model gives a strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programming, Smale's ninth problem. A companion paper constructs polytopes of superpolynomial diameter, disproving the polynomial Hirsch conjecture.

title: Hadwiger's covering conjecture in 3D
why: Dror Aiger, Sariel Har-Peled and Goran Žužić, working with Gemini 4 Carbon, prove Hadwiger's covering conjecture in three dimensions: every convex body can be covered by eight smaller copies of itself. The proof is 13,663 lines of Lean.

title: Sunflower conjecture
why: OpenAI proves the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture for each fixed number of petals: sunflower-free families of equal-size sets are at most exponential in the set size.

title: Protein binders
why: GPT-6.2 designs protein binders through reasoning and code, with specialized biology models filling in structure. 35 of 322 tested by Onava bind their targets, including PD-L1.

title: 1808 fur-trade sketchbook
why: In 22 minutes, GPT-6.2 Astra attributes an anonymous 1808 fur-trade sketchbook at Yale to Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot for historian Mark Humphries. It then locates his 162-page journal on microfilm in Cleveland, whose June 18 entry records the sketch.

title: Integer factoring
why: Gemini 4 gives a factoring algorithm in the number field sieve's subexponential class with no heuristic assumptions. A companion paper gives the first deterministic subexponential factoring algorithm.

title: Discrete logarithms
why: Google's agents compute discrete logarithms in small-characteristic finite fields in better than quasi-polynomial time, unconditionally, improving on the 2014 bound.

title: Log-rank conjecture
why: Gemini 4 breaks the square-root barrier for the log-rank conjecture, the bound Shachar Lovett set in 2014.

title: Edge reconstruction conjecture
why: Gemini 4 proves the edge reconstruction conjecture for every graph with at least 1,000 times as many edges as vertices. Vladimir Müller's 1977 result needed on the order of n log n edges.

title: Approximate Nash equilibria
why: Google's agents find 1/5-approximate Nash equilibria of two-player games in polynomial time. The best guarantee had been about 1/3 since 2007.

title: Hyperlinear and sofic groups
why: Mathematician Peter Burton of the University of Wyoming, with Claude Fable 5.2 writing the Lean proof, constructs a countable group that is hyperlinear but not sofic. It answers Vladimir Pestov's 2008 question of whether every hyperlinear group is sofic.

title: Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis
why: Luke Sernau and colleagues at Anthropic have Claude rewrite Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis in about 76,000 lines, proving the same five theorems. Andrew Sutherland's independent checks at MIT accept it.

title: Quantum gravity from null cones
why: Stanford physicist Venkatesa Chandrasekaran, developing several of the calculations and proofs with GPT-6 Astra, proposes a background-independent quantization of vacuum general relativity in four dimensions. It gives a finite graviton pair amplitude where perturbation theory diverges, then recovers the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy with Sen's one-loop correction.

title: Messages API in Rust
why: Claude rewrites the core of Anthropic's Messages API from Python to Rust in about a week, then Claude agents fix the mismatches found on production traffic. The new API uses about 70% less CPU per request with no downtime.

title: Equiangular lines in dimensions 18 to 20
why: Valjakas Djaljapayan, Zhen-Qi Liao and Wei-Hsuan Yu of National Central University in Taiwan, working with GPT-6, find the maximum number of equiangular lines in dimensions 18, 19 and 20: exactly 57, 72 and 90. The best published upper bounds had been 59, 74 and 94.
